\title{Measuring What Is Missing: Fidelity and Privacy of Missing-Value Patterns in Synthetic Multi-Site Clinical Records}
\titlerunning{Measuring What Is Missing}

% ORCID iDs are optional. Once an author registers at https://orcid.org,

\author{Pranav Ladha \and Devisha Jain \and Nandini Nahata \and Jiya Gakhar}

\begin{abstract}
Clinical tables are incomplete in structured ways: whether a test was done
often depends on the hospital. Recent generators of synthetic patient data
can keep these gaps, but there is no standard way to check that the gaps
are \emph{realistic}, and no study of whether keeping them \emph{leaks} who
was in the training data. We propose missing-value fidelity scores
(per-column and per-site missing rates, and the distribution of whole
missingness patterns), each calibrated against the gap between two real
samples, and a privacy audit that attacks patients through their
missingness patterns. We apply both to MedTwin, a conditional WGAN-GP that
generates a ``measured'' flag per incomplete column for a given hospital,
and to CTGAN, TVAE and TabDDPM, on four-site UCI heart disease (920
patients) and Pima diabetes (768) data over five seeds with held-out
patients. MedTwin's missingness patterns are almost as close to the real
data as a second real sample (pattern distance 0.174 vs.\ 0.152;
baselines 0.209--0.683), and it alone matches per-site missing rates.
Keeping gaps has a small, consistent privacy cost: a membership attack on
patients with rare patterns rises from AUC 0.531 to 0.575, while overall
privacy is unchanged. MedTwin also has the highest fidelity, the least
detectable records on heart disease (61.5\% vs.\ 74.9--92.8\%) and utility
matching the best baseline.
\keywords{Synthetic data \and Generative adversarial networks \and Missing data \and Electronic health records \and Privacy evaluation}
\end{abstract}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Introduction}

Machine learning for clinical prediction depends on access to patient data
that privacy law and institutional policy rightly restrict. Synthetic data,
meaning records drawn from a generative model trained on real patients, is
one proposed way to share such data~\cite{goncalves2020synthetic,yan2022benchmark},
and CTGAN~\cite{xu2019ctgan}, TVAE~\cite{xu2019ctgan} and
TabDDPM~\cite{kotelnikov2023tabddpm} are widely used tabular generators
for it.

Clinical tables are rarely complete, and the gaps follow a pattern. In the UCI heart disease data~\cite{janosi1989heart}, collected at
four hospitals for Detrano et al.~\cite{detrano1989}, every Swiss patient has a serum
cholesterol of 0 (the test was not recorded), the number of major vessels
coloured by fluoroscopy is missing for 96--99\% of patients at three of the
four sites, and resting blood pressure is missing for 28\% of VA Long Beach
patients but almost no one elsewhere. A faithful synthetic version of this
cohort has to reproduce \emph{which} tests were performed \emph{where}.
Most tabular generators need complete input, though, so missing values are
usually imputed first, and the generated cohort then contains invented
measurements that no real record had.

Recent generators can keep missing values in synthetic
data~\cite{bing2022healthgen,ouyang2023missdiff,wang2025reinvented,wang2024igamt}.
Nobody has yet settled how to check whether the generated gaps are
realistic, or whether they leak who was in the training data. A
missingness pattern can identify a patient as well as a value can (think of
the one patient at a site who did have a rare test), but privacy
evaluations of synthetic data only look at values. This paper makes four
contributions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item We define missing-value fidelity scores. They measure how well
  synthetic data reproduces the missing rate of each column, the missing
  rate of each column at each site, and the distribution of whole
  missingness patterns. Each score sits next to a real-vs-real reference
  (the gap between held-out and training patients), which tells the reader
  what a good value looks like.
\item We audit whether keeping gaps exposes training patients. A
  membership attack is run separately on patients with rare and with common
  missingness patterns, and we check whether a pattern held by only one
  training patient shows up again in the synthetic data.
\item We describe MedTwin, a conditional
  WGAN-GP~\cite{gulrajani2017wgangp} conditioned on the hospital. It
  generates a ``measured'' flag for every incomplete column and a flag for
  values stuck at zero, treats zeros that stand for ``not measured'' as
  gaps, and adds a loss that matches correlations.
\item We compare MedTwin with CTGAN, TVAE and TabDDPM on two datasets over
  five seeds, with held-out patients, paired confidence intervals, an
  ablation of each component and a sensitivity check. Along the way we argue
  that real-vs-synthetic detectability, which some papers report as a
  privacy score, measures realism instead.
\end{enumerate}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Tabular and health-record generators.}
In a GAN~\cite{goodfellow2014gan}, one network learns to produce samples
while a second learns to separate them from real ones, and the two get better
by competing. Replacing the second network's real/fake
decision with an estimate of the Wasserstein distance~\cite{arjovsky2017wgan},
kept smooth by a gradient penalty~\cite{gulrajani2017wgangp}, makes training
much less likely to collapse. medGAN~\cite{choi2017medgan} generated high-dimensional binary and count
EHR features. CTGAN~\cite{xu2019ctgan} handled mixed-type tables with
mode-specific normalisation and a conditional generator trained by
sampling; the same work proposed TVAE. CTAB-GAN~\cite{zhao2021ctabgan}
extended this to mixed and long-tailed variables. Diffusion models now lead
general tabular benchmarks: TabDDPM~\cite{kotelnikov2023tabddpm} combines
Gaussian and multinomial diffusion, and TabSyn~\cite{zhang2024tabsyn} runs
score-based diffusion in a learned latent space. For real EHRs,
EHR-Safe~\cite{yoon2023ehrsafe} addresses heterogeneity, sparsity and
variable-length sequences. MedTwin builds on WGAN-GP~\cite{gulrajani2017wgangp}
with Gumbel-softmax categorical outputs~\cite{jang2017gumbel}.

\paragraph{Missing data.}
GAIN~\cite{yoon2018gain} imputes missing entries adversarially, with a
discriminator that guesses which entries were observed.
MisGAN~\cite{li2019misgan} learns a mask generator alongside the data
generator so that the missingness pattern is itself modelled. More recent
work makes the synthetic records themselves incomplete. HealthGen~\cite{bing2022healthgen} generates medical time series that keep their
informative missingness; MissDiff~\cite{ouyang2023missdiff} trains
diffusion models directly on incomplete tables and shows that
``impute-then-generate'' biases the learned distribution; Wang et
al.~\cite{wang2025reinvented} preserve both the observed and the missing
data distributions in a way that plugs into existing generators;
IGAMT~\cite{wang2024igamt} targets longitudinal records whose
measurements are both incomplete and unevenly timed, and trains with
differential privacy; and Petrakos et al.~\cite{petrakos2025rct} model the
dropout process when synthesising randomised-trial data. MedTwin shares their goal.
It differs in using an explicit site condition for missingness that is
driven by hospital practice, in a simple flag encoding that also works for
zero-coded gaps, and in a controlled ablation of that encoding against
imputation under a multi-seed held-out protocol.

\paragraph{Synthetic data for these datasets.}
Recent studies generated synthetic versions of the same or similar data.
Wan Abu Bakar et al.~\cite{wanabubakar2025ctgan} trained CTGAN on the 303
Cleveland heart disease patients after filling missing values with the most
common value, and report moderate train-on-synthetic, test-on-real accuracy
(56\% on the five-level outcome). Subedi et al.~\cite{subedi2025health}
trained CTGAN on the Pima diabetes data; a random forest fell from 82\%
accuracy on real data to 63\% on synthetic data. Alqulaity and
Yang~\cite{alqulaity2024cgan} gave continuous and categorical columns
separate sub-networks in a conditional GAN and tested it on 218
cardiovascular patients from one hospital, reporting only how closely the
distributions match. Lazzaro et al.~\cite{lazzaro2026bayesian} used
Bayesian networks trained on the Cleveland site to augment heart disease
prediction. Each of these studies uses a single run and fills or drops missing
values. None of them tests on patients the generator never saw, and none
measures privacy. Our evaluation does both, over several seeds, and uses
all four heart disease sites, including the ones where most values are
missing.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
Train-on-synthetic, test-on-real (TSTR) was introduced for medical time
series by Esteban et al.~\cite{esteban2017rcgan}. Alaa et
al.~\cite{alaa2022faithful} separate fidelity, diversity and generalisation
(not copying training records). Distance to closest record is a common
privacy check~\cite{zhao2021ctabgan}, and membership inference attacks on
generative models were shown by LOGAN~\cite{hayes2019logan} and
systematised by GAN-Leaks~\cite{chen2020ganleaks}. Stadler et
al.~\cite{stadler2022groundhog} attacked many generators and found that
the privacy a synthetic release gives varies a lot and is hard to predict in
advance. Passing a few attacks is evidence of privacy, but it does not prove
it. Large comparisons of generators on health
records~\cite{yan2022benchmark,hernandez2025framework}, and the Synthcity
library~\cite{qian2023synthcity}, score each model on realism, usefulness
and privacy. In the study by Hernandez et al., simpler models often did as
well as the elaborate ones on realism and usefulness. Fang et
al.~\cite{fang2025memorization} show that tabular diffusion models memorise
training records, increasingly so with longer training.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Method}

\subsection{Encoding records with their missingness}
\label{sec:encoding}

Each dataset is described by a settings file listing its numeric and
categorical columns, the columns in which 0 means ``not measured'', the
columns with a spike at exactly zero, an optional condition column (the
site), and plausible clinical ranges. A real record $r$ is encoded as
follows.

\emph{Not-measured values.} Zeros in the listed columns become missing.
Every numeric column $j$ that is missing for at least one patient receives
a flag $m_j = 1$ if it was not measured; its value is replaced by the
training median as a placeholder that the flag marks as meaningless.

\emph{Zero spikes.} A Sigmoid output cannot place a point mass on one exact
value, so for each listed column we add a flag $z_j = \mathbb{1}[x_j = 0]$.

\emph{Scaling and categories.} Numeric values are min--max scaled to
$[0,1]$, matching the Sigmoid outputs of the generator. Each categorical
column is one-hot encoded, with ``not measured'' as an extra category.

\emph{Condition.} The site is not generated; it is a one-hot condition
vector $c$. Datasets without a site column use a constant condition, which
reduces the model to an unconditional GAN~\cite{goodfellow2014gan}.

\subsection{Conditional WGAN-GP}

The generator $G(z, c)$ maps noise $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_{128})$ and the
condition through two hidden layers (256 and 512 units, LeakyReLU, batch
normalisation). Its output is split into segments: one Sigmoid segment for
scaled numerics and all flags, and one Gumbel-softmax
segment~\cite{jang2017gumbel} (temperature $\tau = 0.2$) per categorical
column, which is relaxed during training and exactly one-hot when sampling.
The critic $D(x, c)$ scores a record together with its condition (layers of
512 and 256 units, LeakyReLU, dropout 0.3), so it judges whether a record is
realistic \emph{for that site}. Training follows WGAN-GP:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_D = \mathbb{E}[D(\tilde{x}, c)] - \mathbb{E}[D(x, c)]
  + \lambda\, \mathbb{E}\big[(\lVert \nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x}, c) \rVert_2 - 1)^2\big],
\end{equation}
with $\tilde{x} = G(z, c)$ generated for the same sites as the real batch,
$\hat{x}$ interpolated between real and generated records at fixed $c$, and
$\lambda = 10$. The generator loss adds a correlation-matching term,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_G = -\mathbb{E}[D(\tilde{x}, c)]
  + \alpha\, \big\lVert \mathrm{corr}([x, c]) - \mathrm{corr}([\tilde{x}, c]) \big\rVert_F^2 / d^2,
\end{equation}
the mean squared difference between the Pearson correlation matrices of the
real and generated batch (including the condition), with $\alpha = 2$.
Columns that are constant within a batch have no defined correlation and
are excluded; without this, a batch that happens to contain no patients of
a rare category produces NaN gradients that corrupt training.

We train for 600 epochs with batch size 64, five critic updates per
generator update, and Adam~\cite{kingma2015adam} (learning rate $10^{-4}$,
$\beta = (0, 0.9)$). The model is implemented in
PyTorch~\cite{paszke2019pytorch}.

\subsection{Decoding}

To sample $n$ records we draw sites with their training frequencies, so
site proportions match the real data exactly. Numeric outputs are mapped
back to clinical units; a zero flag $\geq 0.5$ sets the value to 0, and a
measurement flag $\geq 0.5$ blanks it (``not measured'' takes precedence).
Records outside the plausible clinical ranges are removed. The ranges
include every measured real value, so no real patient would be
filtered. Values are rounded to their recorded precision (e.g.\ ST
depression to 0.1), with counts and scores clipped to their ranges.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Evaluating Missing Values}
\label{sec:missing-eval}

We call a record's \emph{missingness pattern} the set of its values that are
blank (not measured), together with its site when the data has one. Both
real and synthetic records are compared in the same report form, in which a
blank always means ``not measured''.

\subsection{Fidelity}

Let $\mathcal{R}$ be the real training patients and $\mathcal{S}$ a
synthetic sample. We report three scores, all 0 when $\mathcal{S}$ matches
$\mathcal{R}$:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Rate gap}: the mean over columns of the absolute difference in
  the share of blank values.
\item \emph{Site gap}: the same per site and column, averaged with site
  weights; it catches a model that gets overall rates right but puts the
  gaps at the wrong hospital.
\item \emph{Pattern distance}: the total variation distance between the
  distributions of whole patterns,
  $\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{p} |P_{\mathcal{R}}(p) - P_{\mathcal{S}}(p)|$, which
  also captures which values go missing \emph{together}.
\end{itemize}
These scores depend on sample size, so synthetic data is scored on 20
random subsamples the size of the held-out set and averaged. As a
reference we score the held-out real patients the same way: a synthetic
score close to this \emph{real-vs-real} value is as good as a second
sample of real patients.

\subsection{Privacy}

Members are training patients and non-members are held-out patients, in
equal numbers; results are averaged over 20 random member samples.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Rare- vs.\ common-pattern membership inference.} The
  distance-based membership attack of Sect.~\ref{sec:setup}, evaluated
  separately on patients whose pattern is rare (held by at most 2\% of real
  patients) and on the rest. If keeping gaps exposes unusual patients, the
  attack AUC is higher for rare patterns.
\item \emph{Unique-pattern leak.} For patterns held by exactly one patient,
  the share that reappears in the synthetic data when that patient was a
  member, minus the share when they were held out (0 = no leak).
\end{itemize}
An attacker scoring patients only by how often their pattern occurs in the
synthetic data proved uninformative even for copied records, so we do not
report it.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Datasets.}
\emph{Heart disease} (UCI~\cite{janosi1989heart,detrano1989}) has 920 patients from Cleveland (304), Hungary
(293), VA Long Beach (200) and Switzerland (123), with 7 numeric and 7
categorical columns plus the site; 55.3\% have disease (severity
$> 0$). Five numeric columns are sometimes missing, and missingness is
strongly site-dependent (Sect.~\ref{sec:missingness}). \emph{Pima
diabetes}~\cite{smith1988adap}, taken from OpenML (dataset
37)~\cite{vanschoren2014openml}, has 768 patients with 9 numeric columns and
no site; zeros in glucose, blood pressure, skin fold, insulin and BMI mean
``not measured'' (insulin: 48.7\% of patients), while 0 pregnancies is a
real value. Both datasets run from settings files alone, with no code
changes.

\paragraph{Protocol.}
For each of five seeds, 20\% of patients are held out (stratified on the
outcome) and never seen by any generator; the seed also sets every model's
initialisation. Each model generates 2000 records, which pass through the
same plausibility filter and rounding. We report mean $\pm$ SD over seeds
and compare models seed-by-seed with paired $t$-based 95\% confidence
intervals; a difference is called \emph{clear} when its interval excludes
zero.

\paragraph{Baselines.}
CTGAN and TVAE~\cite{xu2019ctgan} (300 epochs, batch size 100) and TabDDPM
(8000 steps), the last a compact reimplementation of the published
design~\cite{kotelnikov2023tabddpm}. None accepts missing values, so they
receive the same measurement-flag and placeholder encoding as MedTwin and
their flagged values are blanked in the same way; they are unconditional
and generate the site like any other column.

\paragraph{Metrics.}
\emph{Fidelity}: mean histogram overlap (20 bins) between real and
synthetic distributions of four key numeric columns, on measured values.
\emph{Detectability}: held-out accuracy of a random forest~\cite{breiman2001rf} trained to tell
real from synthetic records on a balanced sample (50\% = indistinguishable).
\emph{Utility}: a random forest trained on synthetic (TSTR) or real
training (TRTR) records predicts the binary outcome of held-out patients; we
report TSTR AUC and the ratio TSTR/TRTR. Classifiers and nearest-neighbour
searches use scikit-learn~\cite{pedregosa2011sklearn}. \emph{DCR}: the share of synthetic
records whose nearest real record is a training rather than a held-out
patient, with equally sized real sets (50\% = no memorisation).
\emph{Membership inference}: AUC of an attacker who scores each real patient
by its distance to the nearest synthetic record (0.5 = no leakage).
\emph{Correlation gap}: mean absolute difference between the real
(training) and synthetic Pearson correlation matrices, over all encoded
features (numerics, flags and categories) and, more readably, between the
numeric columns only on measured values.

\paragraph{Detectability is not privacy.}
A generator that copied its training records would be undetectable. We
therefore treat detectability as a realism measure and base privacy
statements only on DCR and membership inference against held-out patients.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Comparison with baselines}

Arrows give the direction of better; $\to$ marks a target value.}

\begin{table}[t]

\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{tables/benchmark_diabetes}}

Tables~\ref{tab:heart} and~\ref{tab:diabetes} summarise the benchmark and
Fig.~\ref{fig:benchmark} shows it for heart disease. On both datasets
MedTwin has the highest fidelity, clearly higher than every baseline in
paired comparisons (by 1.4--13.3 points on heart disease and 2.9--13.1 on
diabetes). On heart disease its records are also the least detectable:
61.5\% against 74.9\% for TabDDPM, 79.5\% for TVAE and 92.8\% for CTGAN,
a clear difference in every paired comparison. Utility matches the
strongest baseline: the TSTR/TRTR AUC ratio is 0.975 (heart disease) and
0.983 (diabetes), with no clear difference from TVAE (0.987, 0.989) and
clearly above CTGAN.

On diabetes, TabDDPM is the least detectable model (55.9\% against 64.0\%
for MedTwin) but memorises its training patients: 60.8\% of its records are
closer to a training than to a held-out patient, and membership inference
reaches an AUC of 0.803 (MedTwin: 51.8\% and 0.494), in line with the
memorisation reported for tabular diffusion models~\cite{fang2025memorization}. For MedTwin, CTGAN and
TVAE, mean DCR stays within 49.7--54.0\% and membership-inference AUC
within 0.494--0.533 on both datasets, and no model produced an exact copy
of a training record: these tests detect no memorisation. They are empirical checks against one
attacker and give no formal guarantee.

\label{sec:missingness}

Table~\ref{tab:missing} gives the missing-value fidelity scores. On heart
disease, MedTwin's patterns are almost as close to the training patients as
a second real sample is (pattern distance 0.174 against a real-vs-real
reference of 0.152), against 0.209 for TVAE, 0.487 for TabDDPM and 0.683
for CTGAN; it is clearly better than every baseline in all five seeds. It is
also the only model whose site gap (0.022) matches the real reference
(0.024); the unconditional baselines put gaps at the wrong hospitals (0.035,
0.101 and 0.131). The ablations show where this comes from. Without the
measurement flags, numeric values are never blank and the pattern distance
jumps to 0.693. Without site conditioning, overall missing rates stay right
(rate gap 0.019) but the site gap and pattern distance worsen clearly (0.028
and 0.223): the hospital is what places each gap. On diabetes, which has no
site, MedTwin again has the lowest pattern distance (0.063; baselines
0.111--0.299; without flags 0.486).

Fig.~\ref{fig:missingness} shows the per-site rates behind these scores.
MedTwin reproduces cholesterol missing for every Swiss patient and 28\% of
VA patients, vessel counts missing almost everywhere except Cleveland, and
thalassemia missing for most Hungarian and VA patients. The largest
deviations are for fasting blood sugar in Switzerland (61\% real, 72\%
synthetic), cholesterol at VA Long Beach (28\% against 35\%) and ST slope in
Switzerland (14\% against 7\%).

\subsection{The privacy cost of keeping missing values}

Keeping gaps has a small cost, and it falls on patients with unusual
patterns. On heart disease about 64 of the 368 attacked patients per draw
have a rare missingness pattern. For them, the membership attack reaches an
AUC of 0.575 against MedTwin, compared with 0.531 for the same model trained
without measurement flags, and it is higher in all five seeds. For
patients with common patterns (0.542 against 0.516) and over all patients
(0.532 against 0.515) the difference is not clear. The attack works through
distances and does not rely on copied patterns. Patterns unique to one patient
reappear no more often when that patient was in training than when they were
held out (unique leak $-4.7 \pm 25.3$ points). Between models the rare-pattern
AUCs (0.50--0.57) do not differ clearly. On diabetes, with only about eight
rare-pattern patients per draw, the audit is inconclusive; there, TabDDPM's
memorisation is visible for all patients alike (AUC 0.80 for common
patterns).

\subsection{Ablations}

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Ablations, mean $\pm$ SD over five seeds. Each row removes one
component from the full model; $^*$ marks a clear paired difference from
the full model (95\% CI excludes 0). Variants that do not apply to a
dataset are omitted.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\centering\scriptsize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.5pt}
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{tables/ablation}}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:ablation} removes one component at a time. Replacing the
measurement flags by median imputation, the usual approach, makes records
far easier to detect (heart disease 62.2\% $\to$ 84.2\%; diabetes
64.0\% $\to$ 81.5\%) while fidelity and utility change little: imputed values
blend into the marginal distributions but produce records unlike any real
patient. Removing the zero flag raises detectability on heart disease to
74.9\%, as the model can no longer place 40\% of ST depression values at
exactly zero, and removing site conditioning raises it to 65.6\%.
Removing the correlation loss changes no realism, utility or privacy
metric, but clearly worsens the correlation gap on both datasets in every
seed: between numeric columns it nearly doubles (heart disease 0.041 $\to$
0.075; diabetes 0.034 $\to$ 0.063), and over all encoded features it grows
from 0.025 to 0.030 and from 0.027 to 0.048. So the loss keeps pairwise structure, which is its job, and costs
nothing elsewhere. No component changes utility, DCR or membership
inference. The components change how real the records look
(detectability and correlations) and leave usefulness and privacy where
they were.

The plausibility filter is not ablated: across all runs it removed no
record, because the Sigmoid outputs map back into the range of the training
data, which lies within the clinical ranges. It is only a safeguard and
plays no part in the results.

\subsection{Sensitivity to hyperparameters}

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Sensitivity of the full model on heart disease to the correlation
weight $\alpha$ (default 2) and the number of training epochs (default
600); $^*$ as in
Table~\ref{tab:ablation}.}
\label{tab:sensitivity}
\centering\scriptsize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.5pt}
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{tables/sensitivity}}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity} varies the two main hand-set hyperparameters on
heart disease. With $\alpha \in \{0.5, 8\}$ or 300 epochs, no metric differs
clearly from the default (the correlation gap was measured for the full
model and its ablation only). Training for 1200 epochs gives the same realism
and utility but starts to memorise: DCR rises from 53.2\% to 55.3\% and
membership-inference AUC from 0.532 to 0.548, both clear in every seed.
Fang et al.~\cite{fang2025memorization} report the same trend with
training length for diffusion models. The results do not depend on these
settings, and 600 epochs is a sensible place to stop.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Discussion and Limitations}

The ablations separate two effects. How incomplete records are
represented drives realism: replacing the measurement flags by imputation
alone raises detectability from 62\% to 84\% on heart disease and from
64\% to 81\% on diabetes, and the zero flag and site conditioning add
further, smaller gains. Imputing missing values, as most pipelines do
before synthesis, yields records that look plausible column by column yet
are easy to tell apart from real ones. MissDiff~\cite{ouyang2023missdiff}
reports the same bias for ``impute-then-generate''. The correlation loss
keeps pairwise structure and leaves the other metrics alone.

The missing-value scores show a difference that standard metrics
miss. CTGAN, TVAE and TabDDPM are given exactly the same measurement flags
as MedTwin, and their overall missing rates are close to real (rate gap
0.028--0.059), yet their missingness patterns are far from real because
nothing ties a gap to its hospital. A report of per-column rates or value distributions alone would not
show this. The privacy audit adds a warning. Keeping realistic gaps
slightly exposes the patients whose gaps are unusual. The effect is small
(AUC 0.575) and does not show up as copied patterns, but these are the
patients a data custodian would worry about most. Merging rare patterns
before release is an obvious fix to try.

This study has limits. Both datasets are small (under 1000 patients)
and single-table; larger and longitudinal EHRs may behave differently. The
missing-value privacy audit needs enough rare-pattern patients: it is
conclusive on heart disease but not on diabetes, and the unique-pattern test
rests on about 14 patterns per draw, so its spread is wide.
Detectability remains well above 50\%, so the synthetic records are still
distinguishable from real ones. Our privacy evidence is empirical (one
distance-based membership attack and DCR), and MedTwin applies no
differential privacy; following Stadler et al.~\cite{stadler2022groundhog},
these results should not be read as a privacy guarantee. TabDDPM is our own
compact reimplementation, and neither TabSyn~\cite{zhang2024tabsyn} nor the
missingness-preserving generators discussed in Sect.~2
(MissDiff~\cite{ouyang2023missdiff}, Wang et al.~\cite{wang2025reinvented})
were included as baselines; that comparison should come next. Finally, generated missingness reproduces
the observed pattern, which here reflects site practice; we make no claim
about the underlying missingness mechanism.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Conclusion}

We proposed scores that measure whether synthetic clinical data has
realistic gaps (per column, per site and as whole patterns, each
against a real-vs-real reference), and an audit of whether those gaps leak training
patients. On two public datasets and five seeds, a site-conditioned
generator, MedTwin, reproduces missingness patterns almost as closely as a
second real sample, while standard generators given the same flags do not.
Keeping gaps has a small privacy cost for patients with rare
patterns, which overall privacy metrics do not show. MedTwin also matches the
best baseline's downstream utility, has the highest fidelity, and is the
least detectable model on the multi-site data. Future work includes
mitigations for rare patterns, larger and longitudinal cohorts, differentially
private training, and comparison with missingness-preserving generators such
as MissDiff~\cite{ouyang2023missdiff}.
